newsitem.title: UK: Opinions divided over cobalt, Gecamines to reopen.
newsitem.headline: Opinions divided over cobalt, Gecamines to reopen.

text.p: The bulls and the bears of the cobalt market failed to agree on the next direction of the price following news that major producer Zaire's Gecamines was to reopen its head offices in Lubumbashi and resume normal business on Monday.

Several traders said that the news was enough to take the froth off high grade material which has been trading above $25 a pound. Others strongly argued that business was still been concluded above this level amid jitters over the next political and economic developments in Zaire.
Upside traders cited brisk Japanese demand and a lack of good Zambian material as a signal to higher prices.
Market talk that Gecamines has declared force majeure was circulating the market, though officials at the mining company were unavailable for comment.
One trader pegged high grade cobalt as high as around $25.50/$26.50.
"There may have been a knee jerk reaction to the news but prices have not dipped below $25 a pound," he said.
Others said that Gecamines announcement had moved the metal used in super-alloys and batteries lower. "The market remained sluggish, though it did drift on Gecamines," one source said.

Gecamines, Zaire's state owned mining company, closed its Lubumbashi headquarters situated in the mineral rich Shaba region on Monday as rebel forces of Laurent Kabila advanced on Zaire's second city.

Several traders had expected the facility to be closed for around a month, though most traders polled by Reuters recently said the mines would not be closed for long as cobalt and copper are hard currency earners for the central African state.
Traders and analyst of the cobalt market will monitor the developments in Zaire closely as the region has huge mineral deposits.
Under President Mobutu Zaire's mining operations lacked capital investment which has seen output in both cobalt and copper drop dramatically.

In the early 1980s cobalt production was around 15,000 tonnes a year, versus current levels of around 5,000 tonnes -- still near a fifth of global production. Output of copper has tumbled from around 500,000 tonnes to near 40,000 over the same period.
Several traders suggested that rebel control of the mining region and Zaire in total could spark overseas investment.

But one trader believed credit lines into Gecamines was still in the hands of Mobutu. "The offices of Gecamines in London and Brussels where financial lines are arranged and are still in the hands of the Mobuto regime," a trader said.
The trader said that confidence from overseas investors is unlikely to peak until stability and total calm is seen in the region.
